final_script.audience: General public with secondary-school science literacy

beats.narration: Researchers ran a randomised, double-blind trial of an experimental drug called CardioRestore-7. Just over twelve hundred adults with stable heart failure took either the drug or a dummy placebo for fifty-two weeks. Neither the patients nor their doctors knew who got which.
beats.on_screen: Title card: CardioRestore-7 trial. 1,204 adults, 52 weeks, drug vs placebo, double-blind.

beats.narration: The question they set out to answer in advance was simple: would fewer people die of heart problems or end up in hospital for heart failure? The answer was no. One hundred eighty-seven of six hundred two on the drug, versus one hundred ninety-three on placebo. That difference is well within chance. The main test failed.
beats.on_screen: Bar comparison 187/602 vs 193/602. Caption: hazard ratio 0.96, 95% CI 0.79-1.17, p = 0.68. Stamp: NO DIFFERENCE.

beats.narration: One smaller measure did shift. People on the drug walked about fourteen metres further in a six-minute walking test. That is a secondary result, it was not corrected for testing many things at once, and fourteen metres may not be something a patient would actually notice.
beats.on_screen: Walking icon with +14 m (95% CI 3 to 25). Label: secondary endpoint, uncertain importance.

beats.narration: There was also a downside. Blood pressure dropped low enough to require cutting the dose in forty-seven people on the drug, compared with twelve on placebo. That is nearly four times as often.
beats.on_screen: Side-by-side figures: 47/602 on drug vs 12/602 on placebo. Label: low blood pressure requiring dose reduction.

beats.narration: So: no benefit on what mattered most, a small uncertain walking gain, and more low blood pressure. CardioRestore-7 is still investigational. No regulator has approved it, and nobody should be asking for it as a treatment. This is a trial result, not medical advice.
beats.on_screen: Summary card: primary endpoint null. Secondary gain uncertain. More hypotension. Investigational, not approved by any regulator.

final_narration:
Researchers ran a randomised, double-blind trial of an experimental drug called CardioRestore-7. Just over twelve hundred adults with stable heart failure took either the drug or a dummy placebo for fifty-two weeks. Neither the patients nor their doctors knew who got which.
The question they set out to answer in advance was simple: would fewer people die of heart problems or end up in hospital for heart failure? The answer was no. One hundred eighty-seven of six hundred two on the drug, versus one hundred ninety-three on placebo. That difference is well within chance. The main test failed.
One smaller measure did shift. People on the drug walked about fourteen metres further in a six-minute walking test. That is a secondary result, it was not corrected for testing many things at once, and fourteen metres may not be something a patient would actually notice.
There was also a downside. Blood pressure dropped low enough to require cutting the dose in forty-seven people on the drug, compared with twelve on placebo. That is nearly four times as often.
So: no benefit on what mattered most, a small uncertain walking gain, and more low blood pressure. CardioRestore-7 is still investigational. No regulator has approved it, and nobody should be asking for it as a treatment. This is a trial result, not medical advice.
